Consult Summary:
38-year-old man with known hypothyroidism on thyroxine presents with 2-month history of profound fatigue, insomnia, low mood, decreased appetite, poor concentration, decreased libido, and exertional shortness of breath that began after starting a new job; will be scheduled for in-person exam and laboratory work-up.

History:
• Chief concern: “Very low energy—hard to get up in the morning” for approximately 2 months.  
• Timeline: Symptoms appeared soon after starting a new job (~2 months ago) and have persisted.  
• Current symptoms  
  – Fatigue and low energy throughout the day.  
  – Difficulty initiating/maintaining sleep.  
  – Poor appetite (“not eating very much”).  
  – Difficulty concentrating; easily distracted.  
  – Low mood (“mood is a bit lower”).  
  – Decreased libido; less interest in sexual activity with spouse.  
  – Exertional shortness of breath during sports that was not present several months ago.  
• No visual changes, no morning erections change, no suicidal ideation or thoughts of self-harm.  
• Review of systems (limited to items discussed)  
  – Positive: fatigue, insomnia, anorexia, low mood, poor concentration, low libido, exertional dyspnea.  
  – Negative: visual disturbance, self-harm thoughts, other family psychiatric illness.

Past Medical History:
• Hypothyroidism ― on chronic thyroxine therapy (dose/route/frequency not documented).  
• No past psychiatric diagnoses reported.  
• No other chronic medical conditions mentioned.

Medications:
• Thyroxine (dose/route/frequency not documented).

Allergies:
• No known drug allergies.

Social History:
• Married.  
• Began a new job 2 months ago (temporal association with symptom onset).  
• Confidential environment for tele-visit.  
• No tobacco, alcohol, or other substance history documented.

Family History:
• Father died by suicide 15 years ago.  
• Otherwise unremarkable; mother alive and well; no siblings.

Physical Examination:
• Tele-consult only; no vitals or physical findings recorded.

Investigations:
• None to date; clinician recommended blood tests at upcoming in-person visit.

Assessment & Plan:
Issue 1: Fatigue, low mood, constitutional symptoms  
  • Assessment: Differential includes major depressive disorder, sub-optimally treated hypothyroidism, and anemia (see below).  
  • Plan:  
    – Arrange in-person GP appointment for complete physical examination.  
    – Order laboratory panel: thyroid function tests, CBC, iron studies, B12/folate, metabolic panel (per clinician’s stated “blood tests”).  
    – Consider depression screening (e.g., PHQ-9) at next visit.  
    – Provide reassurance and outline follow-up.

Issue 2: Known hypothyroidism  
  • Assessment: Possible under-replacement or disease progression contributing to current symptoms.  
  • Plan:  
    – Check serum TSH and free T4 with other labs.  
    – Review levothyroxine dose and adherence at next visit; adjust as indicated.

Issue 3: Mood disturbance / possible depressive disorder  
  • Assessment: Meets several DSM-5 criteria; no suicidality reported.  
  • Plan:  
    – Formal mental-health assessment once medical causes ruled out.  
    – Safety net: patient advised to seek urgent help if suicidal thoughts emerge.  
    – Consider counseling or CBT referral pending evaluation.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx):
1. Major depressive disorder / adjustment disorder – Likelihood: High  
   • Fits low mood, anhedonia (low libido, reduced interest), sleep and appetite disturbance, fatigue, concentration problems; onset after job stress; positive family history of suicide.

2. Sub-optimally treated hypothyroidism – Likelihood: Moderate  
   • Known diagnosis; symptoms overlap (fatigue, low mood, dyspnea, anorexia). Bloodwork needed to confirm thyroid hormone status.

3. Anemia (iron-deficiency or other) – Likelihood: Low-Moderate  
   • Fatigue and exertional dyspnea could be due to anemia, especially with decreased intake; no classic bleeding history noted.

Quality checks (document_quality):
● Missing elements: precise medication dose/frequency, full allergy review beyond drugs, vitals, physical examination findings, lifestyle factors (smoking, alcohol), complete ROS.  
● Conflicts: None significant between transcript and DDx (doctor briefly misheard “hyper-” vs “hypo-”; clarified).  
● Transcript quality: Generally clear; brief freezes and repetitions but did not impede information capture.
